organism: Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus), a lancet-shaped, gram-positive, facultative anaerobic bacterium, usually seen as diplococci. Most strains are encapsulated; the capsular polysaccharide is both the main virulence factor and the basis for serotyping - 100 serotypes were documented as of 2020. Most serotypes can cause serious disease, but only a handful account for most actual infections, and which ones dominate varies by age group and geography.
clinicalFeaturesSummary: The major invasive syndromes are pneumonia, bacteremia, and meningitis. In adults, pneumococcal pneumonia (the most common presentation) has a short incubation of 1-3 days and presents with abrupt fever, chills, pleuritic chest pain, and productive cough; case-fatality for pneumonia with bacteremia is around 10%. Bacteremia without pneumonia (over 5,000 US cases/year) carries about 12% case-fatality; meningitis has roughly 14% case-fatality in adults with common neurologic sequelae among survivors. In children under 2, bacteremia without a known infection site is the most common invasive presentation (about 40% of invasive disease in this age group), followed by bacteremic pneumonia (25%-30%); pneumococcus has become the leading cause of bacterial meningitis in children under 5 since Hib's decline. Pneumococci are also a very common cause of acute otitis media - detected in 24%-31% of middle ear aspirates, with more than 60% of children having had at least one episode by 12 months.
epidemiologySummary: Humans are the only reservoir - the organism lives in the nasopharynx of asymptomatic carriers (5%-90% of healthy people depending on age and setting; 20%-60% of school-age children versus only 5%-10% of adults without children, though up to 50%-60% on some military installations). Transmission is via respiratory droplets or autoinoculation from one's own carried bacteria. Infections are more common in winter and early spring. The period of communicability is unknown but presumed to last as long as the organism is present in respiratory secretions.
secularTrendsSummary: An estimated 31,000+ cases and 3,500+ deaths from invasive pneumococcal disease occurred in the US in 2017, more than half in adults with a vaccine indication. Before routine conjugate vaccination (introduced 2000), children under 5 bore an estimated 17,000 invasive cases and 200 deaths annually, plus about 5 million cases of acute otitis media. PCV7 (2000) drove a 99% decline in invasive disease caused by its 7 covered serotypes in children, partly offset by a rise in non-vaccine serotypes (especially 19A); PCV13 (2010), which added 19A and 5 other serotypes, drove a further 90% decline in PCV13-serotype disease in children, with reductions sustained and not offset by new serotype replacement. Adults have benefited indirectly too - PCV13-serotype disease fell more than 60% among adults 65+ through herd effects of childhood vaccination. Coverage gaps remain: only 24.5% of adults 19-64 at increased risk had been vaccinated as of 2017, and more than 65% of people hospitalized with severe pneumococcal disease had a prior hospitalization in the preceding 3-5 years without having received the vaccine.
vaccineDescription: PPSV23 (Pneumovax 23, licensed 1983, replacing an earlier 14-valent vaccine) is a 23-serotype purified polysaccharide vaccine given IM or subcutaneously with phenol preservative, no adjuvant. Four pneumococcal conjugate vaccines (PCVs) have since been licensed, each covering more or differently chosen serotypes than the last: PCV13 (Prevnar 13, 2010, superseding 7-valent PCV7 from 2000), PCV15 (Vaxneuvance, Merck, 2021), PCV20 (Prevnar 20, Pfizer, 2021), and PCV21 (Capvaxive, Merck, licensed June 2024) - the newest, designed specifically around the serotypes that most commonly cause disease in adults rather than children, and the only one of the four not derived from the pediatric PCV13/PCV7 lineage. All PCVs conjugate capsular polysaccharide to CRM197 (a nontoxic diphtheria toxin variant), are given IM with aluminum phosphate adjuvant, and contain no antibiotic or preservative. Conjugation is what makes PCVs immunogenic in infants and produces a durable T-cell-dependent response, unlike polysaccharide-only PPSV23, which elicits a T-cell-independent response that doesn't reliably 'boost' on revaccination. PCV13 is now largely historical for new vaccinations - PCV15, PCV20, and PCV21 have superseded it in both pediatric and adult recommendations - but it will still appear in many patients' vaccination histories.
vaccinationScheduleSummary: Children: since an October 2024 ACIP update, the routine childhood series (2, 4, 6, and 12-15 months) uses PCV15 or PCV20 rather than PCV13; a child who started with PCV13 can finish the series with either newer product, and PCV13 and PCV15 are considered interchangeable throughout. Adults: since ACIP's October 23, 2024 vote, a single dose of PCV (PCV21, PCV20, or PCV15) is recommended for essentially all PCV-naive adults 50 and older, not just 65+ or 19-64-with-a-risk-condition as before - this was a substantial expansion of the age-based recommendation. If PCV15 is used, a PPSV23 dose should follow at least 1 year later for immunocompetent adults, or at least 8 weeks later for those with an immunocompromising condition, cochlear implant, or CSF leak; PCV21 and PCV20 are given as a single dose with no follow-up PPSV23 needed. Adults 19-49 with a chronic medical condition, CSF leak, cochlear implant, or immunocompromising condition remain eligible under the pre-existing risk-based schedule (see Risk-Based Vaccination), and are reassessed under the age-50 rule once they turn 50. Exact next steps for an adult who already has a partial pneumococcal vaccination history depend heavily on exactly what they've received and when (see Risk-Based Vaccination for Adults 19-64 and Vaccination of Adults 50 and Older) - PCV and PPSV23 should never be given on the same clinic day, and when both are needed, PCV should always come first.
vaccineEfficacySummary: PPSV23: more than 80% of healthy adults develop antibody to covered serotypes within 2-3 weeks, persisting at least 5 years in healthy adults but declining faster in those with chronic illness or immunodeficiency; overall clinical effectiveness against invasive disease from covered serotypes is 60%-70%. Antibody response in children under 2 is generally poor, and revaccination doesn't reliably boost titers given the T-cell-independent immune response. There's no consensus PPSV23 prevents non-bacteremic pneumonia, so providers should avoid calling it simply a 'pneumonia vaccine.' PCV13, the original conjugate vaccine, reduced invasive disease from its covered serotypes by 97% in a landmark pediatric trial and showed 45.6%-75.0% efficacy against vaccine-type pneumococcal pneumonia and invasive disease in a large adult trial. The newer PCV15 and PCV20 met noninferiority immunogenicity criteria against PCV13 for shared serotypes in adult trials, with PCV20 additionally meeting noninferiority against PPSV23 for six of seven non-PCV13 serotypes; PCV21 met noninferiority against PCV20 for 10 of 10 shared serotypes and showed statistically higher responses for 10 of 11 of its unique serotypes. Exact duration of protection from any of the newer PCVs, and whether adults will eventually need a booster dose, remains under active study - CDC and ACIP have flagged this as a monitoring priority rather than a settled question.
contraindicationsSummary: A severe allergic reaction to a vaccine component or a prior dose is a contraindication for both PCV and PPSV23. Because all PCVs are conjugated to CRM197, a nontoxic genetically altered diphtheria toxin, they are additionally contraindicated for anyone with a severe allergic reaction history to any diphtheria toxoid-containing vaccine. Moderate or severe acute illness is a precaution. ACIP has no specific recommendation on PCV use during pregnancy; PPSV23 safety in pregnancy hasn't been formally studied, though no adverse outcomes have been reported after inadvertent vaccination - women at increased risk who are vaccine candidates should ideally be vaccinated before becoming pregnant.
vaccineSafetySummary: PPSV23: local reactions (pain, soreness, swelling, induration), headache, fatigue, and muscle pain are most common, usually resolving within 48 hours; adults 65+ tend to have more systemic reactions after a second dose than a first. A transient increase in viral replication has been reported in HIV-positive people after PPSV23, without associated clinical or immunologic deterioration. PCV13 (still relevant for anyone with it in their vaccination history): local reactions plus decreased appetite, fatigue, headache, muscle pain, irritability, and fever (plus altered sleep in infants/toddlers) are most common; simultaneous PCV13 and inactivated influenza vaccine in young children has been associated with an increased febrile-seizure risk in some influenza seasons, though the seizures are brief with no long-term complications and this has not changed vaccination recommendations. PCV15 and PCV21 trials found no vaccine-related serious adverse events (PCV21 trials had reported two in earlier analyses, though this remains a low-certainty signal). PCV20 has a confirmed Guillain-Barre syndrome safety signal: VAERS reporting was low overall (0.7 cases per million doses distributed), but a CMS Medicare-data analysis found a statistically significant GBS signal in adults 65+ using the primary case definition - though the signal lost statistical significance under an alternative GBS definition and after adjusting for diagnostic-code accuracy in sensitivity analyses. CDC and FDA continue to monitor this signal; it has not changed the PCV20 recommendation.
vaccineStorageSummary: PCV13 and PPSV23 must be stored at refrigerator temperature, 2C to 8C (36F to 46F). See CDC's Vaccine Storage and Handling Toolkit for complete guidance.
surveillanceSummary: Invasive pneumococcal disease is notifiable in most states. Definitive diagnosis relies on culturing the organism from blood or another normally sterile site; a urinary antigen test is also available for adult community-acquired pneumonia and can detect infection even after antibiotics have started. See CDC's Manual for the Surveillance of Vaccine-Preventable Diseases for reporting guidance.

supplementalTopics.title: Risk-Based Vaccination for Children and Adolescents
supplementalTopics.summary: Beyond the routine PCV15/PCV20 series in early childhood, children 2 years and older with certain conditions need additional doses. A CSF leak or cochlear implant warrants PCV (PCV15 or PCV20, following the vaccination history the child already has) plus PPSV23 at least 8 weeks later, at any age. Functional/anatomic asplenia (including sickle cell disease) or an immunocompromising condition (congenital/acquired immunodeficiency, malignancy on immunosuppressive therapy, HIV, chronic renal failure, nephrotic syndrome, organ transplant, or immunosuppressive medication) warrants the same PCV-then-PPSV23 sequence PLUS a second PPSV23 dose 5 years after the first. Chronic heart/lung disease, diabetes, chronic liver disease, or (in adults) smoking or alcoholism only trigger a PPSV23 recommendation, not an additional PCV dose, in the 2-18 age range specifically (unlike the same conditions in adults 19-64, where a single PPSV23 dose still applies) - PCV is not indicated for these conditions once a child is out of the routine vaccination age window. PCV21 is not licensed in children and is an adult-only product.

supplementalTopics.title: Risk-Based Vaccination for Adults 19-49
supplementalTopics.summary: Routine PCV/PPSV23 vaccination is not recommended for healthy adults 19-49 (this age band shrank from 19-64 after the October 2024 expansion - see Vaccination of Adults 50 and Older). Unvaccinated adults 19-49 with chronic heart/lung disease, diabetes, chronic liver disease, smoking, or alcoholism should get a single dose of PCV21, PCV20, or PCV15 (with PPSV23 following at least 1 year later if PCV15 was used) - when they turn 50 their pneumococcal vaccination status should be reassessed under the age-based rule. Unvaccinated adults 19-49 with an immunocompromising condition, CSF leak, or cochlear implant should get the same PCV21/20/15 options, with PPSV23 at least 8 weeks later if PCV15 was used (or a single dose of PCV21/20 at least 1 year after a lone prior PPSV23 dose); those with a prior PCV13-only history should get PCV21 or PCV20 at least 1 year later, and PPSV23 is no longer recommended as an option to complete a PCV13-started series. Asplenia or an immunocompromising condition still triggers a second PPSV23 dose 5 years after the first, same as before.

supplementalTopics.title: Vaccination of Adults 50 and Older
supplementalTopics.summary: Since ACIP's October 23, 2024 vote, every PCV-naive adult 50 or older (not just 65+) should receive a single dose of PCV21, PCV20, or PCV15 (with PPSV23 following at least 1 year later, or 8 weeks for those with an immunocompromising condition/cochlear implant/CSF leak, if PCV15 was used). What to do next depends heavily on prior vaccination history: someone with PPSV23 only needs a PCV dose at least 1 year later; someone with PCV13 only needs PCV21 or PCV20 at least 1 year later (PPSV23 is no longer an option to complete that series); someone who completed PCV13 plus PPSV23 before age 65 needs PCV21 or PCV20 at least 5 years after their last dose; and someone who completed PCV13 plus PPSV23 with the PPSV23 dose given at 65 or older is offered PCV21 or PCV20 via shared clinical decision-making, at least 5 years after their last dose, since that combination was already the complete pre-2024 recommended series. Self-reported PPSV23 history (though not PCV history) remains acceptable evidence of vaccination for adults, unlike the written documentation normally required for other vaccines.

supplementalTopics.title: Choosing a Vaccine Where Serotype 4 Disease Is Common
supplementalTopics.summary: PCV21 was deliberately designed around the serotypes that most commonly cause adult disease, and covers 8 serotypes none of the other recommended vaccines include - but it notably does NOT include serotype 4, which PCV15, PCV20, and PPSV23 all cover. In most of the US this doesn't matter, but in populations where serotype 4 causes 30% or more of invasive pneumococcal disease - documented in parts of Alaska, Colorado, Navajo Nation, New Mexico, and Oregon, often concentrated among adults under 65 with alcoholism, chronic lung disease, smoking, homelessness, or injection drug use - PCV20 alone, or PCV15 followed by PPSV23, is expected to give broader protection against locally circulating strains than PCV21 would. This guidance is specifically regional and population-dependent, and CDC expects to revise it as pneumococcal disease epidemiology continues to evolve.

supplementalTopics.title: Timing Around Elective Procedures
supplementalTopics.summary: When a splenectomy, immunocompromising therapy, or cochlear implant placement is being planned, vaccines should ideally be completed before the procedure - PCV first, then PPSV23 at least 8 weeks later if PCV15 was used, with PPSV23 given at least 2 weeks before the treatment or surgery itself if there isn't time for the full 8-week gap. If treatment or surgery can't be delayed, vaccination can be given afterward instead. A person scheduled for splenectomy should be treated as already asplenic for purposes of applying these recommendations.

keyPoints: S. pneumoniae was first isolated by Louis Pasteur in 1881, but wasn't reliably distinguished from other pneumonias until the Gram stain (1884)
PCV and PPSV23 must never be given on the same clinic visit - when both are needed, PCV always comes first
Since October 2024, ACIP recommends PCV for all PCV-naive adults 50 and older, a major expansion from the prior 65+-or-19-64-with-risk-condition rule
Four PCV products now exist (PCV13, PCV15, PCV20, PCV21); PCV21 is the newest and the only one designed specifically around adult, not pediatric, disease serotypes

PCV21 omits serotype 4 coverage that PCV15/PCV20/PPSV23 all include - in regions (Alaska, Colorado, Navajo Nation, New Mexico, Oregon) with high serotype-4 burden, PCV20 alone or PCV15+PPSV23 is preferred instead

PCV20 carries a confirmed but disputed Guillain-Barre syndrome signal - statistically significant in one Medicare-data analysis but not in a sensitivity analysis using a stricter case definition; ACIP has not changed its recommendation because of it
PPSV23 is no longer recommended as an option to complete a series someone started with PCV13 - only PCV21 or PCV20 now fills that role

Racial disparities persist in both pneumococcal disease burden and vaccination coverage: Black and American Indian/Alaska Native adults have higher invasive disease rates and lower vaccination rates than the national average, a factor ACIP explicitly weighed in expanding the age-50 recommendation
Childhood conjugate vaccination has produced substantial indirect (herd) protection in adults 65+ through reduced transmission
Providers should avoid calling PPSV23 a 'pneumonia vaccine' - there's no consensus it prevents non-bacteremic pneumococcal pneumonia specifically
